n: Chapters 50–51 are a long prophecy against Babylon itself—the empire God had used to punish Judah. In scripture Babylon also becomes a symbol of the wicked world; the Lord in our day says, “Go ye out from Babylon.”

f.g: The great capital on the Euphrates, in today’s Iraq; also a scriptural symbol of worldliness.

n: Proclaim it to the nations—raise a banner and hold nothing back: Babylon is captured! Her chief gods Bel and Marduk are humiliated, her idols smashed.

f.g: “Lord”—a title of Marduk, Babylon’s chief god.
Marduk, patron god of Babylon.
Raise a signal flag on a hill to announce news.

n: A nation from the north will come against Babylon and make its land desolate; people and animals will flee. Historically, the Medes and Persians, from the north and east, conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

f.w: out of the north there cometh up a nation

n: At that time Israel and Judah will come together, weeping as they go, seeking the Lord their God. Babylon’s fall opens the way for repentance and return.
They will ask the way to Zion, facing toward it, and say, “Come, let’s bind ourselves to the Lord in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.”

f.g: Toward that place.

n: God’s people have been lost sheep; their own shepherds led them astray to wander from mountain to hill—places of idol worship—and they forgot their true resting place, the Lord.

f.w: My people hath been lost sheep

n: Whoever found them devoured them, saying, “We’re not guilty—they sinned against the Lord, their true pasture and their ancestors’ hope.” Even enemies recognized Israel had abandoned its God.

f.g: Righteous pasture—the Lord as Israel’s true home.

n: Flee from Babylon! Leave the land of the Chaldeans, and be like the male goats that lead the flock out first. Be among the first to leave.

f.w: Remove out of the midst of Babylon

f.g: Lead goats that go out ahead of the flock.

n: God will raise up a coalition of great nations from the north against Babylon. Their archers are expert—no arrow comes back empty.

f.g: Like a skilled warrior whose arrows always hit.

n: Babylonia will be plundered, and its plunderers will have their fill.
Because you rejoiced as you plundered God’s inheritance, frisking like a heifer in the grass and snorting like stallions…

f.g: Israel, God’s own inheritance.
Or “neigh like stallions.”

n: …your “mother” (Babylon) will be humiliated. She will become the last of the nations—a wilderness, dry land, and desert.

f.g: The least or last of the nations.

n: Because of God’s wrath, Babylon will be uninhabited; passersby will be shocked and hiss at its wounds. Babylon did decline over centuries and was eventually abandoned.

f.w: every one that goeth by Babylon shall be astonished

n: Archers, take your positions around Babylon and shoot—spare no arrows—because she sinned against the Lord.
Raise the battle cry! She surrenders; her towers fall and walls are torn down. This is the Lord’s vengeance—do to her as she did to others.

f.g: She has surrendered (literally “given the hand” in submission).

f.w: as she hath done, do unto her

n: Cut off the farmers who sow and harvest in Babylon. Foreigners living there will flee home from the oppressor’s sword.

f.w: they shall turn every one to his people

n: Israel is a scattered sheep chased by lions: first Assyria devoured the northern kingdom (722 BC), and finally Nebuchadnezzar gnawed its bones (586 BC).

f.w: first the king of Assyria hath devoured him

n: So God will punish Babylon’s king and land as he punished Assyria’s king. Assyria’s capital Nineveh fell in 612 BC.

f.w: as I have punished the king of Assyria

n: God will bring Israel home to graze on rich pastures—Carmel, Bashan, the hills of Ephraim, and Gilead.

f.g: Lush pastures west and east of the Jordan.

n: In that day, if anyone searches for Israel’s sin, none will be found, because God will forgive the remnant he preserves. Complete forgiveness through the Atonement is the heart of restoration.

f.w: the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none

f.g: The remnant God spares.

n: Attack the land of Merathaim and the people of Pekod—destroy them completely, as God commands. Both names are wordplays on real Babylonian places.

f.g: “Double rebellion”—a pun on a region in southern Babylonia (mat marratim, “land of the bitter waters”).
“Punishment”—a pun on the Puqudu, an Aramean tribe in eastern Babylonia.

n: The noise of battle and great destruction fills the land.
How the “hammer of the whole earth” is shattered! Babylon, which smashed other nations, is itself broken.

f.w: the hammer of the whole earth

n: God set a trap and Babylon was caught unaware, because she fought against the Lord. According to ancient historians, Babylon fell in 539 BC with surprisingly little resistance.
The Lord opened his armory and brought out the weapons of his wrath—the armies he uses for his purposes.
Come from the farthest borders, break open her granaries, pile her up like heaps of grain, and destroy her completely.
Kill all her young bulls—her warriors—let them go down to slaughter. Their day of reckoning has come.

f.g: Young bulls—a picture of her strong young soldiers.

n: Listen: refugees escaping Babylon arrive in Zion announcing that the Lord has avenged his temple, which Babylon destroyed.
Summon archers to surround Babylon so none escape. Repay her for her deeds, because she defied the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

f.g: A favorite title of God in Isaiah; Latter-day Saints understand it as a name of Jesus Christ.

n: Her young men will fall in the streets and her soldiers be silenced.

f.w: her young men fall in the streets

n: “I am against you, O Pride,” says God—Babylon is so proud that “Pride” becomes her name. Her day of reckoning has come.

f.g: Hebrew zadon, “Arrogance”—used as a name for Babylon.

n: Pride will stumble and fall with no one to lift it up; God will set fire to its cities.

f.w: the most proud shall stumble and fall

n: Israel and Judah have both been oppressed; their captors hold them tightly and refuse to let them go—like Pharaoh in Egypt.

f.w: they refused to let them go

n: But their Redeemer is strong—the Lord of hosts is his name. He will plead their case, bringing rest to his people and unrest to Babylon. Latter-day Saints see in “Redeemer” a title of Jesus Christ.

f.g: Hebrew go’el—the kinsman who buys back and defends a family member.
Thoroughly.

n: A sword on the Chaldeans, on Babylon’s people, its officials, and its wise men! (A poem of repeated “sword” lines, each one falling on a different pillar of Babylon’s pride.)

f.g: Babylon was famed for its astrologers and scholars.

n: A sword on her false prophets, who will be exposed as fools; a sword on her warriors, who will be terrified.

f.g: Diviners or omen-readers who made false predictions.
Become foolish.

n: A sword on her horses, chariots, and foreign mercenaries, who will lose their courage; a sword on her treasures, which will be plundered.

f.g: Foreign troops and residents.
An ancient idiom for losing courage in battle.

n: A drought on her waters to dry them up. Babylon depended on the Euphrates and its canals; the Greek historian Herodotus says Cyrus diverted the river to enter the city. God says it is because Babylon is a land of idols—people obsessed with them.

f.w: A drought is upon her waters
they are mad upon their idols
f.g: They are infatuated with frightful images.

n: Desert creatures, hyenas, and ostriches will live there; it will never again be inhabited.

f.w: the wild beasts of the islands
f.g: Probably hyenas or jackals.
Probably ostriches.

n: Like Sodom and Gomorrah, Babylon will be overthrown and no one will live there.

f.w: As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah

n: A people from the north, a great nation, and many kings are rising from the far ends of the earth.

f.w: Behold, a people shall come from the north

n: Armed with bows and spears, cruel and merciless, roaring like the sea and riding horses in battle formation—against you, daughter Babylon. These same words once described Babylon’s attack on Jerusalem (6:22-23); now the tables are turned.

f.w: they are cruel, and will not shew mercy

n: Babylon’s king hears the news and goes limp; anguish seizes him like a woman in labor—just as Jerusalem once felt when Babylon came.
Like a lion from the Jordan thickets attacking a secure pasture, God will chase Babylon away in an instant. Who is like God? Who can challenge him? (Repeating what was said of Edom in 49:19.)

f.w: he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan

n: Hear God’s plan against Babylon: even the smallest of her flock will be dragged away, and her pastures made desolate.

f.w: the least of the flock shall draw them out

n: At the sound of Babylon’s capture the earth trembles, and the cry is heard among the nations. The empire that seemed eternal falls, as God declared.
